name: Secukinumab
route_note: Subcutaneous injection weekly for loading then every 4 weeks; IV infusion form for PsA and axial spondyloarthritis

discovery.note: Fully human IgG1κ antibody against IL-17A.

tagline: First IL-17A inhibitor, for psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis
summary: Secukinumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that neutralises interleukin-17A. It was the first IL-17 inhibitor approved and is used in plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, enthesitis-related arthritis and hidradenitis suppurativa.
mechanism: IL-17A, produced by Th17 cells, γδ T cells and innate lymphoid cells under the influence of IL-23, acts on keratinocytes, synoviocytes and endothelium to induce chemokines, antimicrobial peptides and inflammatory mediators.

Secukinumab binds IL-17A and blocks its interaction with the IL-17 receptor, interrupting the IL-23/IL-17 axis that drives psoriatic plaques and enthesitis. IL-17 also protects mucosa against Candida, explaining the increase in mucocutaneous candidiasis.
uses: Moderate to severe plaque psoriasis (adults and children)

history.title: EU and US approval
history.detail: Approved in January in the EU and the US for plaque psoriasis, the first IL-17A inhibitor.

history.title: PsA and AS
history.detail: Approved for psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.

history.title: Paediatric psoriasis
history.detail: FDA approves use in children aged 6 years and older with plaque psoriasis.

history.title: HS and IV form
history.detail: Approved for hidradenitis suppurativa and as an IV infusion for PsA and axSpA.

pk.metabolism: Proteolytic catabolism to peptides and amino acids (no CYP metabolism)
pk.excretion: Not renally excreted as intact antibody; cleared by catabolism and target-mediated uptake

serious: New or worsening inflammatory bowel disease

facts: Secukinumab was the first IL-17A inhibitor approved for psoriasis.
IL-17 inhibitors are generally avoided in patients with inflammatory bowel disease, where trials showed worsening.
